action: Administer intravenous iron replacement
action_detail: In patients with HFrEF and iron deficiency (ferritin <100 mcg/L or 100-300 mcg/L with transferrin saturation <20%) with or without anemia, intravenous iron replacement is reasonable to improve functional status and quality of life. Oral iron is not adequate to treat iron deficiency in HF.
source_text: In patients with HFrEF and iron deficiency with or without anemia, intravenous iron replacement is reasonable to improve functional status and QOL.

action: Do not use erythropoietin-stimulating agents
action_detail: In patients with HF and anemia, erythropoietin-stimulating agents (e.g., darbepoetin alfa) should not be used to improve morbidity and mortality. A randomized trial of darbepoetin alfa showed no benefit and increased thrombotic events including stroke.
source_text: In patients with HF and anemia, erythropoietin-stimulating agents should not be used to improve morbidity and mortality.

action: Uptitrate GDMT to maximally tolerated target dose
action_detail: In patients with HFrEF and hypertension, uptitration of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) to the maximally tolerated target dose is recommended for blood pressure control. Hypertension represents an opportunity to maximize GDMT to goal blood pressures.
source_text: In patients with HFrEF and hypertension, uptitration of GDMT to the maximally tolerated target dose is recommended.

action: Perform formal sleep assessment
action_detail: In patients with HF and suspicion of sleep-disordered breathing, a formal sleep assessment is reasonable to confirm the diagnosis and differentiate between obstructive and central sleep apnea. Decision to refer should be based on clinical judgment, as daytime sleepiness may not reflect the degree of underlying sleep-disordered breathing.
source_text: In patients with HF and suspicion of sleep-disordered breathing, a formal sleep assessment is reasonable to confirm the diagnosis and differentiate between obstructive and central sleep apnea.

action: Consider continuous positive airway pressure
action_detail: In patients with HF and obstructive sleep apnea, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) may be reasonable to improve sleep quality and decrease daytime sleepiness. CPAP has not been shown to affect survival but is associated with better sleep quality and nocturnal oxygenation.
source_text: In patients with HF and obstructive sleep apnea, continuous positive airway pressure may be reasonable to improve sleep quality and decrease daytime sleepiness.

action: Do not use adaptive servo-ventilation
action_detail: In patients with NYHA class II to IV HFrEF and central sleep apnea, adaptive servo-ventilation causes harm. Two RCTs showed increased mortality with adaptive servo-ventilation in this population, supported by meta-analyses.
source_text: In patients with NYHA class II to IV HFrEF and central sleep apnea, adaptive servo-ventilation causes harm.

action: Use SGLT2 inhibitor for hyperglycemia and HF outcomes
action_detail: In patients with HF and type 2 diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitors (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, sotagliflozin) are recommended as first-line agents for hyperglycemia management and to reduce HF-related morbidity and mortality. Two RCTs (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced) in 8474 patients with NYHA II-IV and LVEF <=40% showed reductions in all-cause death (13%), CV death (14%), HF hospitalization (26%), and renal outcomes (38%).
source_text: In patients with HF and type 2 diabetes, the use of SGLT2i is recommended for the management of hyperglycemia and to reduce HF-related morbidity and mortality.

action: Monitor for SGLT2i adverse effects
action_detail: Patients on SGLT2 inhibitors should be closely monitored for potential risks including severe genitourinary infections and, less commonly, diabetic ketoacidosis.
source_text: Patients on SGLT2i should be closely monitored for potential risks, including severe genitourinary infections and, less commonly, diabetic ketoacidosis.

action: Define iron deficiency criteria in HF
action_detail: Iron deficiency in HF is defined as ferritin level <100 mcg/L, or ferritin 100-300 mcg/L with transferrin saturation <20%. Routine baseline assessment of all patients with HF includes evaluation for anemia. Iron deficiency is independently associated with reduced exercise capacity.
source_text: Iron deficiency is usually defined as ferritin level <100 mcg/L or 100 to 300 mcg/L, if the transferrin saturation is <20%.

action: Do not use oral iron supplementation
action_detail: Oral iron supplementation is not adequate to treat iron deficiency in patients with HF due to poor absorption and inadequacy to replete iron stores. The IRONOUT HF trial showed no improvement with oral iron supplementation. Intravenous iron is the appropriate route.
source_text: Oral iron is not adequate to treat iron deficiency anemia in patients with HF. This is attributed to the poor absorption of oral iron and inadequacy of oral iron to replete the iron stores.

action: Initiate chronic anticoagulant therapy
action_detail: Patients with chronic HF with permanent, persistent, or paroxysmal AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of >= 2 (for men) should receive chronic anticoagulant therapy.
source_text: Patients with chronic HF with permanent-persistent-paroxysmal AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of >= 2 (for men) and >= 3 (for women) should receive chronic anticoagulant therapy.

action: Initiate chronic anticoagulant therapy
action_detail: Patients with chronic HF with permanent, persistent, or paroxysmal AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of >= 3 (for women) should receive chronic anticoagulant therapy.
source_text: Patients with chronic HF with permanent-persistent-paroxysmal AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of >= 2 (for men) and >= 3 (for women) should receive chronic anticoagulant therapy.

action: Prefer DOAC over warfarin
action_detail: For patients with chronic HF with permanent, persistent, or paroxysmal AF, direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) is recommended over warfarin in eligible patients. Available DOACs include apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, and dabigatran.
source_text: For patients with chronic HF with permanent-persistent-paroxysmal AF, DOAC is recommended over warfarin in eligible patients.

action: Consider AF ablation for symptom relief
action_detail: For patients with HF and symptoms caused by AF, AF ablation is reasonable to improve symptoms and quality of life. RCTs show ablation may reduce hospitalizations and mortality compared with standard care or amiodarone.
source_text: For patients with HF and symptoms caused by AF, AF ablation is reasonable to improve symptoms and QOL.

action: Consider AV nodal ablation with CRT implantation
action_detail: For patients with AF and LVEF <= 50%, if a rhythm control strategy fails or is not desired and ventricular rates remain rapid despite medical therapy, atrioventricular nodal ablation with implantation of a CRT device is reasonable.
source_text: For patients with AF and LVEF <= 50%, if a rhythm control strategy fails or is not desired, and ventricular rates remain rapid despite medical therapy, atrioventricular nodal ablation with implantation of a CRT device is reasonable.

action: Consider anticoagulation even without additional risk factors
action_detail: For patients with chronic HF and permanent, persistent, or paroxysmal AF, chronic anticoagulant therapy is reasonable for men and women without additional CHA2DS2-VASc risk factors beyond HF itself, as HF is an independent risk factor for stroke.
source_text: For patients with chronic HF and permanent-persistent-paroxysmal AF, chronic anticoagulant therapy is reasonable for men and women without additional risk factors.

action: Conduct multidisciplinary discussion on cancer therapy management
action_detail: In patients who develop cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy or HF, a multidisciplinary discussion involving the patient about the risk-benefit ratio of cancer therapy interruption, discontinuation, or continuation is recommended to improve management.
source_text: In patients who develop cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy or HF, a multidisciplinary discussion involving the patient about the risk-benefit ratio of cancer therapy interruption, discontinuation, or continuation is recommended to improve management.

action: Initiate ARB, ACEi, or beta blocker for asymptomatic cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy
action_detail: In asymptomatic patients with cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy (EF <50%), ARB, ACEi, and beta blockers are reasonable to prevent progression to HF and improve cardiac function.
source_text: In asymptomatic patients with cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy (EF <50%), ARB, ACEi, and beta blockers are reasonable to prevent progression to HF and improve cardiac function.

action: Perform pretherapy cardiac function evaluation
action_detail: In patients with cardiovascular risk factors or known cardiac disease being considered for potentially cardiotoxic anticancer therapies, pretherapy evaluation of cardiac function is reasonable to establish baseline cardiac function and guide the choice of cancer therapy. Echocardiography is recommended as the first-line modality for LVEF assessment.
source_text: In patients with cardiovascular risk factors or known cardiac disease being considered for potentially cardiotoxic anticancer therapies, pretherapy evaluation of cardiac function is reasonable to establish baseline cardiac function and guide the choice of cancer therapy.

action: Monitor cardiac function during cardiotoxic cancer therapy
action_detail: In patients with cardiovascular risk factors or known cardiac disease receiving potentially cardiotoxic anticancer therapies, monitoring of cardiac function is reasonable for the early identification of drug-induced cardiomyopathy.
source_text: In patients with cardiovascular risk factors or known cardiac disease receiving potentially cardiotoxic anticancer therapies, monitoring of cardiac function is reasonable for the early identification of drug-induced cardiomyopathy.

action: Consider beta blockers and ACEi/ARB for primary prevention of drug-induced cardiomyopathy
action_detail: In patients at risk of cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy, initiation of beta blockers and ACEi/ARB for the primary prevention of drug-induced cardiomyopathy is of uncertain benefit. Selected beta blockers studied include carvedilol and nebivolol. Spironolactone has also been investigated.
source_text: In patients at risk of cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy, initiation of beta blockers and ACEi/ARB for the primary prevention of drug-induced cardiomyopathy is of uncertain benefit.

action: Consider serial cardiac troponin measurement for risk stratification
action_detail: In patients being considered for potentially cardiotoxic therapies, serial measurement of cardiac troponin might be reasonable for further risk stratification. An elevated pretreatment troponin (>14 ng/L) was associated with a 4-fold increase in risk of cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy.
source_text: In patients being considered for potentially cardiotoxic therapies, serial measurement of cardiac troponin might be reasonable for further risk stratification.

action: Define cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy
action_detail: Cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy is commonly defined as a decrease in LVEF of at least 10 percentage points to below 50%.
source_text: cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy commonly defined as a decrease in LVEF of at least 10% to <50%

action: Discontinue cardiotoxic therapy and initiate GDMT workup
action_detail: Patients who develop HF while receiving potentially cardiotoxic therapies should have these therapies discontinued while a diagnostic workup is undertaken to ascertain the cause of HF and initiate guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT).
source_text: Patients who develop HF while receiving potentially cardiotoxic therapies should have these therapies discontinued while a diagnostic workup is undertaken to ascertain the cause of HF and initiate GDMT.

action: Initiate and uptitrate standard HF therapies for cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy
action_detail: Initiation and uptitration of standard HF therapies (beta blockers, ACEi) remains the mainstay of treatment in patients with cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy or LVEF <50%, with close monitoring of cardiac function to guide discussions with oncology on the resumption of, or choice of, subsequent cancer therapies.
source_text: Initiation and uptitration of standard HF therapies remains the mainstay of treatment in patients with cancer therapy-related cardiomyopathy or LVEF <50%, with close monitoring of cardiac function.

action: Discontinue immune checkpoint inhibitors indefinitely for myocarditis
action_detail: Patients diagnosed with immune checkpoint-related myocarditis typically have the offending agents (nivolumab, ipilimumab, pembrolizumab) discontinued indefinitely, given the associated high mortality.
source_text: patients diagnosed with immune checkpoint-related myocarditis typically have the offending agents discontinued indefinitely, given the associated high mortality.

action: Consider enalapril if post-treatment troponin rises above threshold
action_detail: In patients receiving high-dose chemotherapy with a post-treatment troponin rise >0.07 ng/mL, enalapril was effective in preventing significant LVEF decrease (>10% decrease to below 50%). None of the patients in the enalapril arm met the primary endpoint compared to 43% in the standard of care group.
source_text: 114 patients receiving high-dose chemotherapy and having a posttreatment troponin rise >0.07 ng/mL randomized to enalapril or placebo. None in enalapril arm met the primary endpoint (>10% decrease in LVEF to below 50%), while 43% of placebo group did.

action: Provide patient-centered counseling regarding contraception and pregnancy risks
action_detail: In women with a history of HF or cardiomyopathy, including previous peripartum cardiomyopathy, patient-centered counseling regarding contraception and the risks of cardiovascular deterioration during pregnancy should be provided.
source_text: In women with a history of HF or cardiomyopathy, including previous peripartum cardiomyopathy, patient-centered counseling regarding contraception and the risks of cardiovascular deterioration during pregnancy should be provided.

action: Consider anticoagulation at diagnosis until 6-8 weeks postpartum
action_detail: In women with acute HF caused by peripartum cardiomyopathy and LVEF <30%, anticoagulation may be reasonable at diagnosis, until 6 to 8 weeks postpartum, although the efficacy and safety are uncertain.
source_text: In women with acute HF caused by peripartum cardiomyopathy and LVEF <30%, anticoagulation may be reasonable at diagnosis, until 6 to 8 weeks postpartum, although the efficacy and safety are uncertain.

action: Do not administer ACEi in pregnant women with HF
action_detail: In women with HF or cardiomyopathy who are pregnant or currently planning for pregnancy, ACEi should not be administered because of significant risks of fetal harm. ACEi and ARB are associated with second- and third-trimester renal and tubular dysplasia, oligohydramnios, fetal growth restriction, ossification disorders, lung hypoplasia, and intrauterine fetal death.
source_text: In women with HF or cardiomyopathy who are pregnant or currently planning for pregnancy, ACEi, ARB, ARNi, MRA, SGLT2i, ivabradine, and vericiguat should not be administered because of significant risks of fetal harm.

action: Do not administer ARB in pregnant women with HF
action_detail: In women with HF or cardiomyopathy who are pregnant or currently planning for pregnancy, ARB should not be administered because of significant risks of fetal harm including renal and tubular dysplasia, oligohydramnios, and fetal growth restriction.
source_text: In women with HF or cardiomyopathy who are pregnant or currently planning for pregnancy, ACEi, ARB, ARNi, MRA, SGLT2i, ivabradine, and vericiguat should not be administered because of significant risks of fetal harm.

action: Do not administer ARNi in pregnant women with HF
action_detail: In women with HF or cardiomyopathy who are pregnant or currently planning for pregnancy, ARNi (sacubitril/valsartan) should not be administered because of significant risks of fetal harm. There are no specific data for ARNi in pregnancy.
source_text: In women with HF or cardiomyopathy who are pregnant or currently planning for pregnancy, ACEi, ARB, ARNi, MRA, SGLT2i, ivabradine, and vericiguat should not be administered because of significant risks of fetal harm.

action: Do not administer MRA in pregnant women with HF
action_detail: In women with HF or cardiomyopathy who are pregnant or currently planning for pregnancy, MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone) should not be administered because of significant risks of fetal harm. Spironolactone has sufficient information regarding dose-dependent feminization of male offspring to raise concern.
source_text: For spironolactone, there is sufficient information regarding dose-dependent feminization of male rabbit and rat offspring to raise concern; data are limited for eplerenone.

action: Do not administer SGLT2i in pregnant women with HF
action_detail: In women with HF or cardiomyopathy who are pregnant or currently planning for pregnancy, SGLT2 inhibitors should not be administered because of significant risks of fetal harm.
source_text: In women with HF or cardiomyopathy who are pregnant or currently planning for pregnancy, ACEi, ARB, ARNi, MRA, SGLT2i, ivabradine, and vericiguat should not be administered because of significant risks of fetal harm.

action: Do not administer ivabradine in pregnant women with HF
action_detail: In women with HF or cardiomyopathy who are pregnant or currently planning for pregnancy, ivabradine should not be administered because of significant risks of fetal harm. There are no specific data for ivabradine in pregnancy.
source_text: In women with HF or cardiomyopathy who are pregnant or currently planning for pregnancy, ACEi, ARB, ARNi, MRA, SGLT2i, ivabradine, and vericiguat should not be administered because of significant risks of fetal harm.

action: Do not administer vericiguat in pregnant women with HF
action_detail: In women with HF or cardiomyopathy who are pregnant or currently planning for pregnancy, vericiguat should not be administered because of significant risks of fetal harm.
source_text: In women with HF or cardiomyopathy who are pregnant or currently planning for pregnancy, ACEi, ARB, ARNi, MRA, SGLT2i, ivabradine, and vericiguat should not be administered because of significant risks of fetal harm.

action: Define peripartum cardiomyopathy diagnostic criteria
action_detail: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is defined as systolic dysfunction, typically LVEF <45%, often with LV dilation, occurring in late pregnancy or early postpartum with no other identifiable cardiomyopathy cause.
source_text: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is defined as systolic dysfunction, typically LVEF <45%, often with LV dilation, occurring in late pregnancy or early postpartum with no other identifiable cardiomyopathy cause.

action: Use metoprolol as preferred beta blocker during pregnancy
action_detail: HFrEF medications considered acceptable during pregnancy include beta blockers (most commonly metoprolol), hydralazine, nitrates, and furosemide, within a construct of multidisciplinary shared decision-making regarding benefits and potential risks.
source_text: HFrEF medications considered acceptable during pregnancy, within a construct of multidisciplinary shared decision-making, are furosemide, beta blockers (most commonly metoprolol), hydralazine, and nitrates.

action: Use hydralazine during pregnancy for HF
action_detail: Hydralazine is considered an acceptable HF medication during pregnancy, as part of multidisciplinary shared decision-making regarding benefits and potential risks.
source_text: HFrEF medications considered acceptable during pregnancy, within a construct of multidisciplinary shared decision-making, are furosemide, beta blockers (most commonly metoprolol), hydralazine, and nitrates.

action: Use nitrates during pregnancy for HF
action_detail: Nitrates are considered acceptable HF medications during pregnancy, as part of multidisciplinary shared decision-making regarding benefits and potential risks.
source_text: HFrEF medications considered acceptable during pregnancy, within a construct of multidisciplinary shared decision-making, are furosemide, beta blockers (most commonly metoprolol), hydralazine, and nitrates.

action: Use furosemide during pregnancy for HF with caution
action_detail: Furosemide is considered an acceptable HF medication during pregnancy, with adjustment of diuretic dosing to minimize the risk of placental hypoperfusion.
source_text: HFrEF medications considered acceptable during pregnancy, within a construct of multidisciplinary shared decision-making, are furosemide, beta blockers (most commonly metoprolol), hydralazine, and nitrates.

action: Prefer enalapril or captopril as ACEi during breastfeeding
action_detail: Postpartum women who breastfeed can start ACEi (enalapril or captopril preferred), and metoprolol remains the preferred beta blocker. Monitor neonatal weight with ACEi use and neonatal heart rate with beta blocker use.
source_text: Postpartum women who breastfeed can start ACEi (enalapril or captopril preferred), and metoprolol remains the preferred beta blocker.

action: Consider bromocriptine with prophylactic anticoagulation for severe acute PPCM
action_detail: For postpartum women with severe acute HF caused by peripartum cardiomyopathy and LVEF <35%, bromocriptine may be considered with GDMT pharmacotherapy and prophylactic anticoagulation to improve LVEF recovery. Bromocriptine should be accompanied by at least prophylactic-dosed anticoagulation because of potential hypercoagulability. Efficacy and safety remain uncertain.
source_text: For postpartum women with severe acute HF caused by PPCM and LVEF <35%, in GDMT pharmacotherapy and prophylactic anticoagulation, to improve LVEF recovery; the efficacy and safety of bromocriptine for acute PPCM treatment remains uncertain.

action: Perform echocardiography in third trimester and for symptom changes
action_detail: Consideration of routine echocardiographic screening in the third trimester for reassessment of myocardial structure and function before labor; echocardiography for any significant changes in HF symptoms or signs during pregnancy, or if HF medications are reduced or discontinued.
source_text: Consideration of routine echocardiographic screening in the third trimester for reassessment of myocardial structure and function before labor; echocardiography for any significant changes in HF symptoms or signs during pregnancy.

action: Monitor BNP or NT-proBNP during pregnancy
action_detail: BNP or NT-proBNP monitoring during pregnancy may have some value for prediction of cardiovascular events in women with HF.
source_text: BNP or NT-proBNP monitoring during pregnancy may have some value for prediction of cardiovascular events.

action: Discontinue teratogenic HF medications before conception
action_detail: For women planning pregnancy imminently, modification of HF pharmacotherapy including discontinuation of any ACEi, ARB, ARNi, MRA, SGLT2i, or ivabradine medications. Continue beta blocker (most commonly metoprolol), hydralazine, and nitrates. Adjust diuretic dosing to minimize risk of placental hypoperfusion. Repeat echocardiography approximately 3 months after preconception HF medication adjustments.
source_text: For women planning pregnancy imminently, modification of HF pharmacotherapy including discontinuation of any ACEi, ARB, ARNi, MRA, or SGLT2i or ivabradine medications.

action: Classify HF Stage A as at-risk for HF
action_detail: Stage A (At Risk for HF): Patients at risk for HF but without symptoms, structural heart disease, or cardiac biomarker abnormalities. Therapeutic interventions aim to modify risk factors.
source_text: Therapeutic interventions in each stage aim to modify risk factors (stage A), treat risk and structural heart disease to prevent HF (stage B), and reduce symptoms, morbidity, and mortality (stages C and D).

action: Classify HF Stage B as pre-HF
action_detail: Stage B (Pre-HF): Patients without current or prior symptoms/signs of HF but with evidence of structural heart disease, abnormal cardiac function, or elevated natriuretic peptide levels. Therapeutic interventions aim to treat risk and structural heart disease to prevent HF.
source_text: Therapeutic interventions in each stage aim to modify risk factors (stage A), treat risk and structural heart disease to prevent HF (stage B), and reduce symptoms, morbidity, and mortality (stages C and D).

action: Classify HF Stage C as symptomatic HF
action_detail: Stage C (Symptomatic HF): Patients with current or prior symptoms and/or signs of HF caused by structural and/or functional cardiac abnormality. Therapeutic interventions aim to reduce symptoms, morbidity, and mortality.
source_text: Therapeutic interventions in each stage aim to modify risk factors (stage A), treat risk and structural heart disease to prevent HF (stage B), and reduce symptoms, morbidity, and mortality (stages C and D).

action: Classify HF Stage D as advanced HF
action_detail: Stage D (Advanced HF): Patients with severe symptoms and/or signs of HF at rest, recurrent hospitalizations despite guideline-directed management and therapy. Therapeutic interventions aim to reduce symptoms, morbidity, and mortality.
source_text: Therapeutic interventions in each stage aim to modify risk factors (stage A), treat risk and structural heart disease to prevent HF (stage B), and reduce symptoms, morbidity, and mortality (stages C and D).

action: Use NYHA classification to characterize functional capacity
action_detail: The NYHA classification (Classes I-IV) is used to characterize symptoms and functional capacity of patients with symptomatic HF (Stage C) or advanced HF (Stage D). NYHA class is an independent predictor of mortality and is used to determine eligibility for treatment strategies.
source_text: The NYHA classification is used to characterize symptoms and functional capacity of patients with symptomatic (stage C) HF or advanced HF (stage D). It is an independent predictor of mortality.

action: Maintain Stage C classification despite becoming asymptomatic
action_detail: A patient with symptomatic HF (Stage C) who becomes asymptomatic with treatment (NYHA Class I) should still be categorized as Stage C HF. HF staging does not regress even when symptoms resolve with therapy.
source_text: Although a patient with symptomatic HF (stage C) may become asymptomatic with treatment (NYHA class I), that patient will still be categorized as stage C HF.

action: Classify as HFrEF
action_detail: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is defined as LVEF <= 40%.
source_text: In this guideline, HFrEF is defined as LVEF <= 40% (Table 4).

action: Classify as HFpEF
action_detail: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is defined as LVEF >= 50% with evidence of spontaneous or provokable increased LV filling pressures (e.g., elevated natriuretic peptide, noninvasive/invasive hemodynamic measurement).
source_text: HFpEF: LVEF >= 50% Evidence of spontaneous or provokable increased LV filling pressures (eg, elevated natriuretic peptide, noninvasive and invasive hemodynamic measurement)

action: Classify as HFmrEF
action_detail: Heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) is defined as LVEF 41%-49% with evidence of spontaneous or provokable increased LV filling pressures (e.g., elevated natriuretic peptide, noninvasive/invasive hemodynamic measurement).
source_text: HFmrEF: LVEF 41%-49% Evidence of spontaneous or provokable increased LV filling pressures (eg, elevated natriuretic peptide, noninvasive and invasive hemodynamic measurement)

action: Classify as HFimpEF
action_detail: Heart failure with improved ejection fraction (HFimpEF) is defined as previous LVEF <= 40% and a follow-up measurement of LVEF > 40%. These patients should continue HFrEF treatment.
source_text: HFimpEF: Previous LVEF <= 40% and a follow-up measurement of LVEF >40%

action: Continue HFrEF treatment
action_detail: Patients with HFrEF who improve their LVEF to > 40% are considered to have HFimpEF and should continue HFrEF treatment. EF can decrease after withdrawal of pharmacological treatment in many patients who had improved EF.
source_text: Patients with HFrEF who improve their LVEF to >40% are considered to have HFimpEF and should continue HFrEF treatment.

action: Classify HF Stage A (At Risk)
action_detail: Stage A (At Risk for HF): Patients at risk for HF but without symptoms, structural heart disease, or cardiac biomarkers of stretch or injury (e.g., patients with hypertension, atherosclerotic CVD, diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity, exposure to cardiotoxic agents, genetic variant for cardiomyopathy, or positive family history of cardiomyopathy).
source_text: Stage A: At risk for HF but without symptoms, structural heart disease, or cardiac biomarkers of stretch or injury (eg, patients with hypertension, atherosclerotic CVD, diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity...)

action: Classify HF Stage B (Pre-HF)
action_detail: Stage B (Pre-HF): No symptoms or signs of HF and evidence of one of the following: structural heart disease (reduced LV/RV systolic function, reduced EF, reduced strain, ventricular hypertrophy, chamber enlargement, wall motion abnormalities, valvular heart disease), evidence for increased filling pressures, or risk factors with increased BNP levels or persistently elevated cardiac troponin.
source_text: Stage B: Pre-HF. No symptoms or signs of HF and evidence of 1 of the following: Structural heart disease, Evidence for increased filling pressures, Patients with risk factors and Increased levels of BNPs or Persistently elevated cardiac troponin

action: Classify HF Stage C (Symptomatic HF)
action_detail: Stage C (Symptomatic HF): Structural heart disease with current or previous symptoms of HF. Patients whose symptoms and signs of HF are resolved are still Stage C and should be treated accordingly.
source_text: Stage C: Symptomatic HF. Structural heart disease with current or previous symptoms of HF. Patients whose symptoms and signs of HF are resolved are still stage C and should be treated accordingly.

action: Classify HF Stage D (Advanced HF)
action_detail: Stage D (Advanced HF): Marked HF symptoms that interfere with daily life and with recurrent hospitalizations despite attempts to optimize guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT).
source_text: Stage D: Advanced HF. Marked HF symptoms that interfere with daily life and with recurrent hospitalizations despite attempts to optimize GDMT.

action: Calculate H2FPEF score for HFpEF diagnosis
action_detail: The H2FPEF score integrates predictive variables for diagnosing HFpEF: obesity, atrial fibrillation, age > 60 years, treatment with >= 2 antihypertensive medications, echocardiographic E/e' ratio > 9, and echocardiographic PA systolic pressure > 35 mmHg. Score ranges 0-9. Scores < 2 reflect low likelihood for HFpEF; scores >= 6 reflect high likelihood. Scores 2-5 may require further evaluation with exercise echocardiogram or cardiac catheterization.
source_text: H2FPEF score integrates: obesity, atrial fibrillation, age >60 years, treatment with >= 2 antihypertensive medications, echocardiographic E/e' ratio >9, and echocardiographic PA systolic pressure >35 mm Hg. Scores <2 and >= 6 reflect low and high likelihood for HFpEF.

action: Use elevated E/e' ratio to support diagnosis
action_detail: For HFmrEF and HFpEF diagnosis, evidence of increased LV filling pressures is required. This can be fulfilled with elevated natriuretic peptides, echocardiographic diastolic parameters such as E/e' >= 15, other evidence of elevated filling pressures, or invasive hemodynamic measurement at rest or exercise.
source_text: The criteria can be fulfilled with findings of elevated levels of natriuretic peptides, echocardiographic diastolic parameters such as an E/e' >= 15 or other evidence of elevated filling pressures, or invasive hemodynamic measurement at rest or exercise.

action: Monitor LVEF trajectory over time
action_detail: Patients with HFmrEF are usually in a dynamic trajectory to improvement from HFrEF or to deterioration to HFrEF. One EF measurement at one time point may not be adequate; the trajectory of LVEF over time and the cause is important to evaluate. A significant reduction in LVEF over time is a poor prognostic factor.
source_text: Patients with HFmrEF are usually in a dynamic trajectory to improvement from HFrEF or to deterioration to HFrEF. For patients whose EF falls into this mildly reduced category, 1 EF measurement at 1 time point may not be adequate.

action: Perform exercise echocardiography or cardiac catheterization
action_detail: For patients with H2FPEF scores between 2 and 5 (indeterminate range), further evaluation with exercise echocardiogram or cardiac catheterization is recommended to confirm or negate a diagnosis of HFpEF.
source_text: A score between 2 and 5 may require further evaluation of hemodynamics with exercise echocardiogram or cardiac catheterization to confirm or negate a diagnosis of HFpEF.

action: Assess vital signs and clinical congestion at each encounter
action_detail: In patients with HF, vital signs and evidence of clinical congestion should be assessed at each encounter to guide overall management, including adjustment of diuretics and other medications.
source_text: In patients with HF, vital signs and evidence of clinical congestion should be assessed at each encounter to guide overall management, including adjustment of diuretics and other medications.

action: Assess for clinical factors indicating advanced HF
action_detail: In patients with symptomatic HF, clinical factors indicating the presence of advanced HF should be sought via the history and physical examination. Identification allows earlier referral to an advanced HF center for specialized interventions such as mechanical circulatory support or cardiac transplantation.
source_text: In patients with symptomatic HF, clinical factors indicating the presence of advanced HF should be sought via the history and physical examination.

action: Obtain 3-generation family history for cardiomyopathy
action_detail: In patients with cardiomyopathy, a 3-generation family history should be obtained or updated when assessing the cause of the cardiomyopathy to identify possible inherited disease. A 3-generation pedigree obtained by genetic health care professionals improved the rate of detection of a familial process compared with routine care.
source_text: In patients with cardiomyopathy, a 3-generation family history should be obtained or updated when assessing the cause of the cardiomyopathy to identify possible inherited disease.

action: Perform thorough history and physical to uncover specific HF causes
action_detail: In patients presenting with HF, a thorough history and physical examination should direct diagnostic strategies to uncover specific causes that may warrant disease-specific management, including amyloid heart disease, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, and others.
source_text: In patients presenting with HF, a thorough history and physical examination should direct diagnostic strategies to uncover specific causes that may warrant disease-specific management.

action: Assess cardiac, noncardiac, lifestyle, and social determinants of HF
action_detail: In patients presenting with HF, a thorough history and physical examination should be obtained and performed to identify cardiac and noncardiac disorders, lifestyle and behavioral factors, and social determinants of health that might cause or accelerate the development or progression of HF.
source_text: In patients presenting with HF, a thorough history and physical examination should be obtained and performed to identify cardiac and noncardiac disorders, lifestyle and behavioral factors, and social determinants of health.

action: Perform additional laboratory testing to explore specific HF cause
action_detail: For patients presenting with HF, the specific cause of HF should be explored using additional laboratory testing for appropriate management. Conditions such as ischemic cardiomyopathy, cardiac amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, infectious mechanisms (HIV, COVID-19, Chagas), hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, peripartum cardiomyopathy, cardiotoxicity with cancer therapies, or substance abuse require specific management.
source_text: For patients presenting with HF, the specific cause of HF should be explored using additional laboratory testing for appropriate management.

action: Obtain standard laboratory panel at HF diagnosis
action_detail: For patients who are diagnosed with HF, laboratory evaluation should include complete blood count, urinalysis, serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium), blood urea nitrogen, serum creatinine, glucose, fasting lipid profile, liver function tests, iron studies (serum iron, ferritin, transferrin saturation), and thyroid-stimulating hormone.
source_text: For patients who are diagnosed with HF, laboratory evaluation should include complete blood count, urinalysis, serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, serum creatinine, glucose, lipid profile, liver function tests, iron studies, and thyroid-stimulating hormone.

action: Perform 12-lead ECG at initial HF encounter
action_detail: For all patients presenting with HF, a 12-lead ECG should be performed at the initial encounter. ECG provides important information on rhythm, heart rate, QRS morphology and duration, cause, and prognosis of HF. It is repeated when there is clinical indication such as suspicion for arrhythmia, ischemia, or conduction abnormalities.
source_text: For all patients presenting with HF, a 12-lead ECG should be performed at the initial encounter to optimize management.

action: Measure BNP or NT-proBNP to support diagnosis or exclusion of HF
action_detail: In patients presenting with dyspnea, measurement of BNP or NT-proBNP is useful to support a diagnosis or exclusion of HF. Provides incremental diagnostic value when cause of dyspnea is unclear and physical examination is equivocal. Higher sensitivity than specificity in emergency settings; more useful for ruling out HF than ruling in.
source_text: In patients presenting with dyspnea, measurement of B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or N-terminal prohormone of B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is useful to support a diagnosis or exclusion of HF.

action: Measure BNP or NT-proBNP for risk stratification in chronic HF
action_detail: In patients with chronic HF, measurements of BNP or NT-proBNP levels are recommended for risk stratification. Higher levels are associated with greater risk for adverse short- and long-term outcomes including all-cause and cardiovascular death and major cardiovascular events.
source_text: In patients with chronic HF, measurements of BNP or NT-proBNP levels are recommended for risk stratification.

action: Measure BNP or NT-proBNP at admission for prognosis
action_detail: In patients hospitalized for HF, measurement of BNP or NT-proBNP levels at admission is recommended to establish prognosis. Higher levels are associated with greater risk for adverse short- and long-term outcomes including all-cause and cardiovascular death.
source_text: In patients hospitalized for HF, measurement of BNP or NT-proBNP levels at admission is recommended to establish prognosis.

action: Screen with BNP or NT-proBNP followed by team-based care to prevent HF
action_detail: In patients at risk of developing HF, BNP or NT-proBNP-based screening followed by team-based care including a cardiovascular specialist can be useful to prevent development of LV dysfunction or new-onset HF. In STOP-HF trial, participants with BNP >= 50 pg/mL underwent echocardiography and referral to cardiovascular specialist.
source_text: In patients at risk of developing HF, BNP or NT-proBNP-based screening followed by team-based care, including a cardiovascular specialist, can be useful to prevent the development of LV dysfunction or new-onset HF.

action: Measure predischarge BNP or NT-proBNP to inform trajectory and postdischarge prognosis
action_detail: In patients hospitalized for HF, a predischarge BNP or NT-proBNP level can be useful to inform the trajectory of the patient and establish a postdischarge prognosis. Patients in whom levels decreased with treatment had better outcomes than those without changes or with a biomarker rise. However, targeting a certain threshold or relative change has not been consistently shown to improve outcomes.
source_text: In patients hospitalized for HF, a predischarge BNP or NT-proBNP level can be useful to inform the trajectory of the patient and establish a postdischarge prognosis.

action: Do not use BNP and NT-proBNP values interchangeably
action_detail: BNP and NT-proBNP levels are similar in utility, and either can be used in patient care settings, but their respective absolute values and cut-points must not be used interchangeably. Obesity is associated with lower levels of BNP and NT-proBNP, reducing diagnostic sensitivity.
source_text: BNP and NT-proBNP levels are similar, and either can be used in patient care settings as long as their respective absolute values and cut-points are not used interchangeably.

action: Use BNP threshold >= 50 pg/mL to trigger echocardiography and specialist referral
action_detail: In patients at risk of HF (hypertension, diabetes, or known vascular disease but without established LV systolic dysfunction or symptomatic HF), a BNP level >= 50 pg/mL should trigger echocardiography and referral to a cardiovascular specialist, per STOP-HF trial protocol.
source_text: Participants in the intervention group with BNP levels >= 50 pg/mL underwent echocardiography and referral to a cardiovascular specialist.

action: Perform chest x-ray
action_detail: In patients with suspected or new-onset HF, or those presenting with acute decompensated HF, a chest x-ray should be performed to assess heart size and pulmonary congestion and to detect alternative cardiac, pulmonary, and other diseases that may cause or contribute to symptoms.
source_text: In patients with suspected or new-onset HF, or those presenting with acute decompensated HF, a chest x-ray should be performed to assess heart size and pulmonary congestion and to detect alternative cardiac, pulmonary, and other diseases that may cause or contribute to the patient's symptoms.

action: Perform transthoracic echocardiography
action_detail: In patients with suspected or newly diagnosed HF, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) should be performed during initial evaluation to assess cardiac structure and function.
source_text: In patients with suspected or newly diagnosed HF, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) should be performed during initial evaluation to assess cardiac structure and function.

action: Repeat echocardiography for clinical change or pre-procedure evaluation
action_detail: In patients with HF who have had a significant clinical change, or who have received GDMT and are being considered for invasive procedures or device therapy, repeat measurement of EF, degree of structural remodeling, and valvular function are useful to inform therapeutic interventions. Reevaluation of EF recommended >40 days after MI, >90 days after revascularization, >90 days after GDMT.
source_text: In patients with HF who have had a significant clinical change, or who have received GDMT and are being considered for invasive procedures or device therapy, repeat measurement of EF, degree of structural remodeling, and valvular function are useful.

action: Use alternative imaging when echocardiography is inadequate
action_detail: In patients for whom echocardiography is inadequate, alternative imaging (cardiac magnetic resonance [CMR], cardiac computed tomography [CT], radionuclide imaging) is recommended for assessment of LVEF.
source_text: In patients for whom echocardiography is inadequate, alternative imaging (eg, cardiac magnetic resonance [CMR], cardiac computed tomography [CT], radionuclide imaging) is recommended for assessment of LVEF.

action: Consider CMR for HF or cardiomyopathy diagnosis and management
action_detail: In patients with HF or cardiomyopathy, CMR can be useful for diagnosis or management. CMR provides noninvasive myocardial characterization including late-gadolinium enhancement for fibrosis detection and T1/T2 mapping for infiltrative and inflammatory cardiomyopathies (myocarditis, sarcoidosis, Fabry disease, amyloidosis).
source_text: In patients with HF or cardiomyopathy, CMR can be useful for diagnosis or management.

action: Evaluate for ischemic heart disease as cause of HF
action_detail: In patients with HF, an evaluation for possible ischemic heart disease can be useful to identify the cause and guide management. Noninvasive stress imaging with echocardiography or nuclear scintigraphy can identify patients likely to have obstructive CAD. Invasive or CT coronary angiography can detect and characterize extent of CAD.
source_text: In patients with HF, an evaluation for possible ischemic heart disease can be useful to identify the cause and guide management.

action: Consider noninvasive stress imaging to guide coronary revascularization
action_detail: In patients with HF and coronary artery disease (CAD) who are candidates for coronary revascularization, noninvasive stress imaging (stress echocardiography, SPECT, CMR, or PET) may be considered for detection of myocardial ischemia to help guide coronary revascularization decisions.
source_text: In patients with HF and coronary artery disease (CAD) who are candidates for coronary revascularization, noninvasive stress imaging (stress echocardiography, SPECT, CMR, or PET) may be considered for detection of myocardial ischemia.

action: Do not perform routine repeat LV function assessment without indication
action_detail: In patients with HF, in the absence of: 1) clinical status change, 2) treatment interventions that might have had a significant effect on cardiac function, or 3) candidacy for invasive procedures or device therapy, routine repeat assessment of LV function is not indicated.
source_text: In patients with HF in the absence of: 1) clinical status change, 2) treatment interventions that might have had a significant effect on cardiac function, or 3) candidacy for invasive procedures or device therapy, routine repeat assessment of LV function is not indicated.

action: Consider wireless PA pressure monitoring by implanted hemodynamic monitor
action_detail: In selected adult patients with NYHA class III HF and history of a HF hospitalization in the past year or elevated natriuretic peptide levels, on maximally tolerated stable doses of GDMT with optimal device therapy, the usefulness of wireless monitoring of PA pressure by an implanted hemodynamic monitor to reduce the risk of subsequent HF hospitalizations is uncertain.
source_text: In selected adult patients with NYHA class III HF and history of a HF hospitalization in the past year or elevated natriuretic peptide levels, on maximally tolerated stable doses of GDMT with optimal device therapy, the usefulness of wireless monitoring of PA pressure by an implanted hemodynamic monitor to reduce the risk of subsequent HF hospitalizations is uncertain.

action: Assess cost-effectiveness of wireless PA pressure monitoring
action_detail: In patients with NYHA class III HF with a HF hospitalization within the previous year, wireless monitoring of the PA pressure by an implanted hemodynamic monitor provides uncertain value. Cost-effectiveness analyses show increased survival and QALYs but also increased costs, with estimates ranging from high to intermediate value.
source_text: In patients with NYHA class III HF with a HF hospitalization within the previous year, wireless monitoring of the PA pressure by an implanted hemodynamic monitor provides uncertain value.

action: Assess and document NYHA functional classification
action_detail: In patients with HF, assessment and documentation of NYHA functional classification are recommended to determine eligibility for treatments. NYHA class I: no limitations; class II: slight symptoms with ordinary activity; class III: symptoms with less than ordinary activity; class IV: symptoms at rest.
source_text: In patients with HF, assessment and documentation of NYHA functional classification are recommended to determine eligibility for treatments.

action: Perform cardiopulmonary exercise testing for advanced therapy candidacy
action_detail: In selected ambulatory patients with HF, cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) is recommended to determine appropriateness of advanced treatments such as LVAD and heart transplant.
source_text: In selected ambulatory patients with HF, cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) is recommended to determine appropriateness of advanced treatments (eg, LVAD, heart transplant).

action: Perform CPET or 6-minute walk test to assess functional capacity
action_detail: In ambulatory patients with HF, performing a cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) or 6-minute walk test is reasonable to assess functional capacity.
source_text: In ambulatory patients with HF, performing a CPET or 6-minute walk test is reasonable to assess functional capacity.

action: Perform CPET to evaluate cause of unexplained dyspnea
action_detail: In ambulatory patients with unexplained dyspnea, cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) is reasonable to evaluate the cause of dyspnea. CPET can help distinguish respiratory versus cardiac etiologies of dyspnea.
source_text: In ambulatory patients with unexplained dyspnea, CPET is reasonable to evaluate the cause of dyspnea.

action: Consider heart transplant listing based on peak VO2
action_detail: Peak VO2 <= 14 mL/kg/min is the cutoff to distinguish patients who may derive survival benefit from heart transplant. Patients with peak VO2 >14 mL/kg/min who were deferred had 1- and 2-year survival of 94% and 84%, respectively, similar to survival after heart transplant.
source_text: Patients with peak VO2 <=14 mL/kg/min were listed for transplant... the authors proposed peak VO2 <= 14 mL/kg/min as a cutoff to distinguish patients who may derive survival benefit from heart transplant.

action: Consider heart transplant listing for patients on beta blockers based on adjusted peak VO2 cutoff
action_detail: For patients on beta blockers, a peak VO2 <= 12 mL/kg/min has been suggested as a more appropriate cutoff to consider cardiac transplant listing, as patients tolerating beta blockers may have improved survival with an equivalent VO2 compared with patients who do not tolerate beta blockers.
source_text: For patients on beta blockers, a peak VO2 <=12 mL/kg/min has been suggested as a more appropriate cutoff to consider cardiac transplant listing.

action: Identify high-risk HF patients based on 6-minute walk test distance
action_detail: A 6-minute walk test distance <300 m roughly correlates to patients with NYHA class III to IV symptoms and is associated with worse 3-year survival free of heart transplant (62% versus 82% for those walking >= 300 m).
source_text: A cutoff of <300 m roughly correlates to patients with NYHA class III to IV symptoms and is associated with worse 3-year survival free of heart transplant (62% versus 82% for those walking >= 300 m).

action: Use validated multivariable risk scores to estimate mortality risk
action_detail: In ambulatory or hospitalized patients with HF, validated multivariable risk scores can be useful to estimate subsequent risk of mortality. Commonly used scores include the Seattle Heart Failure Model, Heart Failure Survival Score, and MAGGIC score for chronic HF; PARADIGM-HF and HF-ACTION for HFrEF; I-PRESERVE and TOPCAT for HFpEF; and ADHERE CART, AHA GWTG, EFFECT, and ESCAPE scores for acute decompensated HF.
source_text: In ambulatory or hospitalized patients with HF, validated multivariable risk scores can be useful to estimate subsequent risk of mortality.

action: Control blood pressure per GDMT
action_detail: In patients with hypertension, blood pressure should be controlled in accordance with guideline-directed medical therapy for hypertension to prevent symptomatic HF. Target SBP <130/80 mmHg for those with CVD risk >=10%. SBP goal <120 mmHg decreased incident HF by 38% (SPRINT trial).
source_text: In patients with hypertension, blood pressure should be controlled in accordance with GDMT for hypertension to prevent symptomatic HF.

action: Prescribe SGLT2 inhibitor to prevent HF hospitalization
action_detail: In patients with type 2 diabetes and either established CVD or at high cardiovascular risk, SGLT2 inhibitors should be used to prevent hospitalizations for HF. Benefit is independent of glucose lowering. Not evaluated in severe renal impairment (eGFR <25 mL/min/1.73 m2).
source_text: In patients with type 2 diabetes and either established CVD or at high cardiovascular risk, SGLT2i should be used to prevent hospitalizations for HF.

action: Maintain healthy lifestyle habits
action_detail: In the general population, healthy lifestyle habits such as regular physical activity, maintaining normal weight, healthy dietary patterns (Mediterranean, DASH diet), and avoiding smoking are helpful to reduce future risk of HF and preserve cardiac structure.
source_text: In the general population, healthy lifestyle habits such as regular physical activity, maintaining normal weight, healthy dietary patterns, and avoiding smoking are helpful to reduce future risk of HF.

action: Screen with natriuretic peptide biomarkers and refer to cardiovascular specialist
action_detail: For patients at risk of developing HF, natriuretic peptide biomarker-based screening (BNP >=50 pg/mL triggers echocardiography and cardiovascular specialist referral) followed by team-based care optimizing GDMT can be useful to prevent LV dysfunction (systolic or diastolic) or new-onset HF.
source_text: For patients at risk of developing HF, natriuretic peptide biomarker-based screening followed by team-based care, including a cardiovascular specialist optimizing GDMT, can be useful to prevent the development of LV dysfunction or new-onset HF.

action: Use validated multivariable risk scores to estimate incident HF risk
action_detail: In the general population, validated multivariable risk scores (Framingham Heart Failure Risk Score, Health ABC Heart Failure Score, ARIC Risk Score, PCP-HF) can be useful to estimate subsequent risk of incident HF. PCP-HF provides race- and sex-specific 10-year risk equations using age, blood pressure, fasting glucose, BMI, cholesterol, smoking status, and QRS duration.
source_text: In the general population, validated multivariable risk scores can be useful to estimate subsequent risk of incident HF.

action: SGLT2 inhibitors not evaluated in severe renal impairment
action_detail: SGLT2 inhibitors have not been evaluated in patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR <25 mL/min/1.73 m2). Use in this population lacks evidence.
source_text: SGLT2i are generally well tolerated, but these agents have not been evaluated in those with severe renal impairment (estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] <25 mL/min/1.73 m2).

action: Perform echocardiography and refer to cardiovascular specialist
action_detail: In patients at risk for HF with BNP levels >=50 pg/mL, echocardiography and referral to a cardiovascular specialist should be performed to evaluate for asymptomatic LV dysfunction (systolic or diastolic). This reduced composite endpoint of asymptomatic LV dysfunction with or without newly diagnosed HF (STOP-HF trial).
source_text: screening with BNP testing and then intervening on those with levels of >= 50 pg/mL (performing echocardiography and referral to a cardiovascular specialist) reduced the composite endpoint of asymptomatic LV dysfunction with or without newly diagnosed HF.

action: Prescribe ACE inhibitor
action_detail: In patients with LVEF <= 40% (Stage B pre-HF), ACE inhibitors should be used to prevent symptomatic HF and reduce mortality.
source_text: In patients with LVEF <= 40%, ACEi should be used to prevent symptomatic HF and reduce mortality.

action: Prescribe statin after MI or ACS
action_detail: In patients with a recent or remote history of MI or ACS, statins should be used to prevent symptomatic HF and adverse cardiovascular events.
source_text: In patients with a recent or remote history of MI or ACS, statins should be used to prevent symptomatic HF and adverse cardiovascular events.

action: Prescribe ARB if ACEi intolerant post-MI
action_detail: In patients with a recent MI and LVEF <= 40% who are intolerant to ACE inhibitors, ARB should be used to prevent symptomatic HF and reduce mortality.
source_text: In patients with a recent MI and LVEF <= 40% who are intolerant to ACEi, ARB should be used to prevent symptomatic HF and reduce mortality.

action: Prescribe evidence-based beta blocker post-MI
action_detail: In patients with a recent or remote history of MI or ACS and LVEF <= 40%, evidence-based beta blockers should be used to reduce mortality.
source_text: In patients with a recent or remote history of MI or ACS and LVEF <= 40%, evidence-based beta blockers should be used to reduce mortality.

action: Implant ICD for primary prevention of SCD post-MI
action_detail: In patients who are at least 40 days post-MI with LVEF <= 30% and NYHA class I symptoms while receiving GDMT and have reasonable expectation of meaningful survival for >1 year, an ICD is recommended for primary prevention of sudden cardiac death to reduce total mortality.
source_text: In patients who are at least 40 days post-MI with LVEF <= 30% and NYHA class I symptoms while receiving GDMT...an ICD is recommended for primary prevention of SCD to reduce total mortality.

action: Prescribe beta blocker to prevent symptomatic HF
action_detail: In patients with LVEF <= 40% (including those without history of MI), beta blockers should be used to prevent symptomatic HF.
source_text: In patients with LVEF <= 40%, beta blockers should be used to prevent symptomatic HF.

action: Avoid thiazolidinediones
action_detail: In patients with LVEF < 50%, thiazolidinediones should not be used because they increase the risk of HF, including hospitalizations. Associated with fluid retention and increased rates of HF.
source_text: In patients with LVEF <50%, thiazolidinediones should not be used because they increase the risk of HF, including hospitalizations.

action: Avoid nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
action_detail: In patients with LVEF < 50%, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) with negative inotropic effects may be harmful.
source_text: In patients with LVEF <50%, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers with negative inotropic effects may be harmful.

action: Provide multidisciplinary team care
action_detail: Patients with HF should receive care from multidisciplinary teams to facilitate the implementation of GDMT, address potential barriers to self-care, reduce the risk of subsequent rehospitalization for HF, and improve survival.
source_text: Patients with HF should receive care from multidisciplinary teams to facilitate the implementation of GDMT, address potential barriers to self-care, reduce the risk of subsequent rehospitalization for HF, and improve survival.

action: Provide HF self-care education and support
action_detail: Patients with HF should receive specific education and support to facilitate HF self-care in a multidisciplinary manner, including medication adherence, sodium restriction, physical activity, and symptom monitoring.
source_text: Patients with HF should receive specific education and support to facilitate HF self-care in a multidisciplinary manner.

action: Vaccinate against respiratory illnesses
action_detail: In patients with HF, vaccinating against respiratory illnesses (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19) is reasonable to reduce mortality. Influenza vaccination was associated with significant reductions in all-cause mortality and cardiovascular mortality.
source_text: In patients with HF, vaccinating against respiratory illnesses is reasonable to reduce mortality.

action: Screen for depression, social isolation, frailty, and low health literacy
action_detail: In adults with HF, screening for depression, social isolation, frailty, and low health literacy as risk factors for poor self-care is reasonable to improve management. Tools include PHQ-9 for depression, Fried frailty phenotype for frailty, SAHL/REALM-SF for health literacy.
source_text: In adults with HF, screening for depression, social isolation, frailty, and low health literacy as risk factors for poor self-care is reasonable to improve management.

action: Avoid excessive sodium intake
action_detail: For patients with stage C HF, avoiding excessive sodium intake is reasonable to reduce congestive symptoms. AHA recommends reduction of sodium intake to less than 2300 mg/d for general cardiovascular health, though no trials support this specific threshold in HF. Aggressive sodium restriction (0.8 g/d) has not shown benefit.
source_text: For patients with stage C HF, avoiding excessive sodium intake is reasonable to reduce congestive symptoms.

action: Recommend exercise training or regular physical activity
action_detail: For patients with HF who are able to participate, exercise training (or regular physical activity) is recommended to improve functional status, exercise performance, and quality of life. Benefits include improved endothelial function, blunted catecholamine spillover, increased peripheral oxygen extraction, and improvement in peak oxygen consumption.
source_text: For patients with HF who are able to participate, exercise training (or regular physical activity) is recommended to improve functional status, exercise performance, and QOL.

action: Refer to cardiac rehabilitation program
action_detail: In patients with HF, a cardiac rehabilitation program can be useful to improve functional capacity, exercise tolerance, and health-related quality of life. Program includes medical evaluation, education regarding medical adherence, dietary recommendations, psychosocial support, and exercise training.
source_text: In patients with HF, a cardiac rehabilitation program can be useful to improve functional capacity, exercise tolerance, and health-related QOL.

action: Initiate diuretics for congestion relief
action_detail: In patients with HF who have fluid retention, diuretics are recommended to relieve congestion, improve symptoms, and prevent worsening HF.
source_text: In patients with HF who have fluid retention, diuretics are recommended to relieve congestion, improve symptoms, and prevent worsening HF.

action: Add thiazide to loop diuretic for diuretic resistance
action_detail: For patients with HF and congestive symptoms, addition of a thiazide (e.g., metolazone) to treatment with a loop diuretic should be reserved for patients who do not respond to moderate- or high-dose loop diuretics to minimize electrolyte abnormalities.
source_text: For patients with HF and congestive symptoms, addition of a thiazide (eg, metolazone) to treatment with a loop diuretic should be reserved for patients who do not respond to moderate- or high-dose loop diuretics to minimize electrolyte abnormalities.

action: Prefer loop diuretics as first-line diuretic
action_detail: Loop diuretics are the preferred diuretic agents for use in most patients with HF. The most commonly used loop diuretic is furosemide, but some patients respond more favorably to bumetanide or torsemide due to increased oral bioavailability.
source_text: Loop diuretics are the preferred diuretic agents for use in most patients with HF. The most commonly used loop diuretic for the treatment of HF is furosemide, but some patients respond more favorably to other agents (eg, bumetanide, torsemide).

action: Consider thiazide diuretics for hypertensive HF with mild fluid retention
action_detail: Thiazide diuretics such as chlorthalidone or hydrochlorothiazide may be considered in patients with hypertension and HF and mild fluid retention.
source_text: Thiazide diuretics such as chlorthalidone or hydrochlorothiazide may be considered in patients with hypertension and HF and mild fluid retention.

action: Dose bumetanide for chronic HF congestion
action_detail: Bumetanide: initial daily dose 0.5-1.0 mg once or twice daily; maximum total daily dose 10 mg; duration of action 4-6 hours.
source_text: Bumetanide: Initial Daily Dose 0.5-1.0 mg once or twice, Maximum Total Daily Dose 10 mg, Duration of Action 4-6 h.

action: Dose furosemide for chronic HF congestion
action_detail: Furosemide: initial daily dose 20-40 mg once or twice daily; maximum total daily dose 600 mg; duration of action 6-8 hours.
source_text: Furosemide: Initial Daily Dose 20-40 mg once or twice, Maximum Total Daily Dose 600 mg, Duration of Action 6-8 h.

action: Dose torsemide for chronic HF congestion
action_detail: Torsemide: initial daily dose 10-20 mg once daily; maximum total daily dose 200 mg; duration of action 12-16 hours.
source_text: Torsemide: Initial Daily Dose 10-20 mg once, Maximum Total Daily Dose 200 mg, Duration of Action 12-16 h.

action: Dose chlorothiazide for chronic HF congestion
action_detail: Chlorothiazide: initial daily dose 250-500 mg once or twice daily; maximum total daily dose 1000 mg; duration of action 6-12 hours.
source_text: Chlorthiazide: Initial Daily Dose 250-500 mg once or twice, Maximum Total Daily Dose 1000 mg, Duration of Action 6-12 h.

action: Dose chlorthalidone for chronic HF congestion
action_detail: Chlorthalidone: initial daily dose 12.5-25 mg once daily; maximum total daily dose 100 mg; duration of action 24-72 hours.
source_text: Chlorthalidone: Initial Daily Dose 12.5-25 mg once, Maximum Total Daily Dose 100 mg, Duration of Action 24-72 h.

action: Dose hydrochlorothiazide for chronic HF congestion
action_detail: Hydrochlorothiazide: initial daily dose 25 mg once or twice daily; maximum total daily dose 200 mg; duration of action 6-12 hours.
source_text: Hydrochlorothiazide: Initial Daily Dose 25 mg once or twice, Maximum Total Daily Dose 200 mg, Duration of Action 6-12 h.

action: Dose indapamide for chronic HF congestion
action_detail: Indapamide: initial daily dose 2.5 mg once daily; maximum total daily dose 5 mg; duration of action 36 hours.
source_text: Indapamide: Initial Daily Dose 2.5 mg once, Maximum Total Daily Dose 5 mg, Duration of Action 36 h.

action: Dose metolazone for chronic HF congestion
action_detail: Metolazone: initial daily dose 2.5 mg once daily; maximum total daily dose 20 mg; duration of action 12-24 hours.
source_text: Metolazone: Initial Daily Dose 2.5 mg once, Maximum Total Daily Dose 20 mg, Duration of Action 12-24 h.

action: Always combine diuretics with other GDMT
action_detail: Diuretics should not be used in isolation but always combined with other guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for HF that reduces hospitalizations and prolongs survival. With the exception of MRAs, the effects of diuretics on morbidity and mortality are uncertain.
source_text: Diuretics should not be used in isolation but always combined with other GDMT for HF that reduces hospitalizations and prolongs survival. With the exception of MRAs, the effects of diuretics on morbidity and mortality are uncertain.

action: Titrate diuretics to euvolemia using lowest effective dose
action_detail: The treatment goal of diuretic use is to eliminate clinical evidence of fluid retention, using the lowest dose possible to maintain euvolemia. In outpatients with HF, diuretic therapy is commonly initiated with low doses and the dose is increased until urine output increases and weight decreases, generally by 0.5 to 1.0 kg daily.
source_text: The treatment goal of diuretic use is to eliminate clinical evidence of fluid retention, using the lowest dose possible to maintain euvolemia...dose is increased until urine output increases and weight decreases, generally by 0.5 to 1.0 kg daily.

action: Avoid NSAIDs with diuretics due to reduced efficacy
action_detail: Patients may become unresponsive to high doses of diuretic drugs if they are taking agents that can block the effects of diuretics (e.g., NSAIDs).
source_text: Patients may become unresponsive to high doses of diuretic drugs if they are taking agents that can block the effects of diuretics (eg, NSAIDs).

action: Consider vasopressin antagonists for hyponatremia in HF
action_detail: If reversing potential causes and free water restriction do not improve hyponatremia, vasopressin antagonists may be helpful in the acute management of volume overload to decrease congestion while maintaining serum sodium.
source_text: If reversing potential causes and free water restriction do not improve hyponatremia, vasopressin antagonists may be helpful in the acute management of volume overload to decrease congestion while maintaining serum sodium.

action: Monitor for electrolyte abnormalities with combination diuretic therapy
action_detail: The addition of metolazone to loop diuretics was found to increase the risk for hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and worsening renal function. Monitor electrolytes closely when using combination diuretic therapy.
source_text: The addition of metolazone to loop diuretics was found to increase the risk for hypokalemia, hyponatremia, worsening renal function, and mortality.

action: Prescribe ARNi
action_detail: In patients with HFrEF and NYHA class II to III symptoms, the use of ARNi (sacubitril-valsartan) is recommended to reduce morbidity and mortality.
source_text: In patients with HFrEF and NYHA class II to III symptoms, the use of ARNi is recommended to reduce morbidity and mortality.

action: Prescribe ACEi when ARNi not feasible
action_detail: In patients with previous or current symptoms of chronic HFrEF, the use of ACEi is beneficial to reduce morbidity and mortality when the use of ARNi is not feasible.
source_text: In patients with previous or current symptoms of chronic HFrEF, the use of ACEi is beneficial to reduce morbidity and mortality when the use of ARNi is not feasible.

action: Prescribe ARB when ACEi intolerant and ARNi not feasible
action_detail: In patients with previous or current symptoms of chronic HFrEF who are intolerant to ACEi because of cough or angioedema and when the use of ARNi is not feasible, the use of ARB is recommended to reduce morbidity and mortality.
source_text: In patients with previous or current symptoms of chronic HFrEF who are intolerant to ACEi because of cough or angioedema and when the use of ARNi is not feasible, the use of ARB is recommended to reduce morbidity and mortality.

action: Use ACEi or ARB for high economic value when ARNi not feasible
action_detail: In patients with previous or current symptoms of chronic HFrEF, in whom ARNi is not feasible, treatment with an ACEi or ARB provides high economic value.
source_text: In patients with previous or current symptoms of chronic HFrEF, in whom ARNi is not feasible, treatment with an ACEi or ARB provides high economic value.

action: Switch from ACEi or ARB to ARNi
action_detail: In patients with chronic symptomatic HFrEF NYHA class II or III who tolerate an ACEi or ARB, replacement by an ARNi is recommended to further reduce morbidity and mortality.
source_text: In patients with chronic symptomatic HFrEF NYHA class II or III who tolerate an ACEi or ARB, replacement by an ARNi is recommended to further reduce morbidity and mortality.

action: Prefer ARNi over ACEi for high economic value
action_detail: In patients with chronic symptomatic HFrEF, treatment with an ARNi instead of an ACEi provides high economic value.
source_text: In patients with chronic symptomatic HFrEF, treatment with an ARNi instead of an ACEi provides high economic value.

action: Do not co-administer ARNi with ACEi
action_detail: ARNi should not be administered concomitantly with ACEi or within 36 hours of the last dose of an ACEi. Concomitant use can lead to angioedema.
source_text: ARNi should not be administered concomitantly with ACEi or within 36 hours of the last dose of an ACEi.

action: Do not administer ARNi in patients with history of angioedema
action_detail: ARNi should not be administered to patients with any history of angioedema due to concern for increased risk of recurrence.
source_text: ARNi should not be administered to patients with any history of angioedema.

action: Do not administer ACEi in patients with history of angioedema
action_detail: ACEi should not be administered to patients with any history of angioedema. ARB do not interfere as directly with bradykinin metabolism and may be considered as an alternative.
source_text: ACEi should not be administered to patients with any history of angioedema.

action: Start ACEi at low dose and titrate upward
action_detail: ACEi should be started at low doses and titrated upward to doses shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in clinical trials. Give with caution if low systemic blood pressure, renal insufficiency, or elevated serum potassium (>5.0 mEq/L). If maximal doses not tolerated, use intermediate doses; avoid abrupt withdrawal.
source_text: ACEi should be started at low doses and titrated upward to doses shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in clinical trials.

action: Start ARB at low dose and titrate upward
action_detail: ARB should be started at low doses and titrated upward, with an attempt to use doses shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in clinical trials. Give with caution if low systemic blood pressure, renal insufficiency, or elevated serum potassium (>5.0 mEq/L).
source_text: ARB should be started at low doses and titrated upward, with an attempt to use doses shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in clinical trials.

action: Allow 36-hour washout between ACEi and ARNi
action_detail: If patients are switched from an ACEi to an ARNi or vice versa, there should be at least 36 hours between ACEi and ARNi doses to reduce risk of angioedema.
source_text: If patients are switched from an ACEi to an ARNi or vice versa, there should be at least 36 hours between ACEi and ARNi doses.

action: Initiate ARNi de novo before hospital discharge for acute HF
action_detail: ARNi should be initiated de novo in patients hospitalized with acute HFrEF before discharge in the absence of contraindications, given improvement in health status, reduction in NT-proBNP, and improvement of LV remodeling parameters compared with ACEi/ARB.
source_text: ARNi should be initiated de novo in patients hospitalized with acute HFrEF before discharge in the absence of contraindications.

action: Monitor blood pressure, renal function, and potassium with RAS inhibitors
action_detail: ACEi and ARB should be given with caution to patients with low systemic blood pressure, renal insufficiency, or elevated serum potassium (>5.0 mEq/L). ARNi is more frequently associated with symptomatic hypotension.
source_text: ACEi and ARB should be given with caution to patients with low systemic blood pressure, renal insufficiency, or elevated serum potassium (>5.0 mEq/L).

action: Prescribe evidence-based beta blocker
action_detail: In patients with HFrEF with current or previous symptoms, use one of the 3 beta blockers proven to reduce mortality: bisoprolol, carvedilol, or sustained-release metoprolol succinate. This is recommended to reduce mortality and hospitalizations.
source_text: In patients with HFrEF, with current or previous symptoms, use of 1 of the 3 beta blockers proven to reduce mortality (eg, bisoprolol, carvedilol, sustained-release metoprolol succinate) is recommended to reduce mortality and hospitalizations.

action: Recognize high economic value of beta-blocker therapy
action_detail: In patients with HFrEF with current or previous symptoms, beta-blocker therapy provides high economic value. Multiple analyses confirm cost-effectiveness using generic beta-blocker costs.
source_text: In patients with HFrEF, with current or previous symptoms, beta-blocker therapy provides high economic value.

action: Do not substitute non-evidence-based beta blockers
action_detail: Only bisoprolol, sustained-release metoprolol succinate, and carvedilol are recommended for HFrEF. The favorable findings with these 3 agents should not be considered a beta-blocker class effect. Other beta blockers are not included in this recommendation for use.
source_text: The favorable findings with these 3 agents, however, should not be considered a beta-blocker class effect in HFrEF. Other beta blockers are not included in this recommendation for use.

action: Initiate beta blocker even when asymptomatic
action_detail: Even when asymptomatic, or when symptoms are mild or improve with other therapies, beta-blocker therapy is important and should not be delayed until symptoms return or disease progression is documented.
source_text: Even when asymptomatic, or when symptoms are mild or improve with other therapies, beta-blocker therapy is important and should not be delayed until symptoms return or disease progression is documented.

action: Initiate beta blocker before hospital discharge
action_detail: Beta blockers can be safely initiated before hospital discharge, provided patients are clinically stabilized and do not require intravenous inotropic therapy for HF.
source_text: Data show that beta blockers can be safely initiated before hospital discharge, provided patients are clinically stabilized and do not require intravenous inotropic therapy for HF.

action: Start beta blocker at low dose and titrate to target
action_detail: Beta blockers should be initiated at low doses, and every effort should be made to achieve the target doses of the beta blockers shown to be effective in major clinical trials, as tolerated.
source_text: Beta blockers should be initiated at low doses, and every effort should be made to achieve the target doses of the beta blockers shown to be effective in major clinical trials, as tolerated.

action: Maintain long-term beta-blocker therapy even if LVEF improves
action_detail: Even if symptoms or LVEF improve, long-term treatment with beta blockers and use of target doses should be maintained to reduce the risk of progression in LV dysfunction or major cardiovascular events.
source_text: Even if symptoms or LVEF improve, long-term treatment with beta blockers and use of target doses should be maintained to reduce the risk of progression in LV dysfunction or major cardiovascular events.

action: Avoid abrupt withdrawal of beta-blocker therapy
action_detail: Abrupt withdrawal of beta-blocker therapy can lead to clinical deterioration and should be avoided unless indicated.
source_text: Abrupt withdrawal of beta-blocker therapy can lead to clinical deterioration and should be avoided unless indicated.

action: Document contraindication or intolerance and retry later
action_detail: If a contraindication or intolerance to beta blockers is noted, it should be documented, and the patient should be restarted on beta-blocker therapy in the future, so long as an absolute contraindication is not present.
